item.title: We know how to hurt India, says Pakistan coach Solano ahead of SAFF Championship final. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan head coach Nolberto Solano believes his side has what it takes to trouble India in the SAFF Championship final, insisting that his players must focus on their own strengths rather than become preoccupied with their opponents as the two arch-rivals prepare for a historic showdown on Tuesday.

Pakistan will face defending champions India at the National Stadium in Dhaka, Bangladesh, with the Green Shirts chasing their maiden SAFF Championship title and a landmark first appearance in the tournament’s final.

Speaking at the pre-match press conference on Monday, Solano acknowledged India’s quality but maintained that Pakistan had studied their opponents and understood where they could make an impact.

“We all prepare. It’s a final match, and we respect India. We are always checking and looking, but in football there are no more secrets,” Solano said.

“You know how they play. The most important thing is to focus on ourselves, on what we want to do, because we know our strengths and how we can hurt India.”

The Peruvian coach described the encounter as a special occasion and a derby, recognising the significance of a Pakistan-India contest, particularly with silverware at stake.

However, he stressed that his team’s attention must remain on executing its own game plan rather than allowing the occasion or the opposition to dictate its approach.

‘Football history’

For Pakistan, Tuesday’s final represents an opportunity to turn an encouraging tournament campaign into one of the most significant achievements in the country’s football history.

The Green Shirts booked their place in the showpiece match with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over hosts Bangladesh in Saturday’s semi-final. Abdul Samad Arshad scored the decisive goal in the closing stages to send Pakistan into their first-ever SAFF Championship final.

Their progress has been particularly noteworthy given the limited preparation time and the difficulties surrounding the availability of several overseas-based players during the group stage.

Pakistan’s final opponents, meanwhile, are pursuing a historic achievement of their own. India have won the SAFF Championship nine times and will be looking to secure an unprecedented third consecutive title, having lifted the trophy in the previous two editions.

The final will be a rematch of the Group ‘B’ encounter between the two sides on Nov 5, when India secured a 3-2 victory after establishing a commanding three-goal advantage.

Suhail Ahmad Bhat scored twice, while Manglenthang Kipgen added India’s third as Pakistan struggled to find their rhythm during the opening half.

The Green Shirts responded with two goals in stoppage time, including a spectacular overhead kick from Alamgir Ghazi, but their late rally proved insufficient to prevent defeat.

Solano admitted that Pakistan’s slow start and lack of concentration had contributed to the result, while also pointing to the difficult journey and inadequate preparation time before their opening fixture.

“I don’t like to make excuses, but we had a very bad journey before we arrived, and we faced them without two days of training. In the first 45 minutes, we weren’t focused. We were quite slow, so they took their chances and scored,” he said.

The coach, however, was encouraged by his side’s response after the interval, believing Pakistan had shown enough improvement to suggest they could compete more effectively in the rematch.

“In the second half, we improved and played much better. We could have come back into the match, but we did it a little bit late. That’s why we lost 3-2. But it’s another game, a different game,” Solano added.

Pakistan’s squad has since received a significant boost with the arrival of several overseas-based players who were unavailable during the group stage because the tournament fell outside the FIFA international window.

Captain Abdullah Iqbal, Easah Suliman, Adil Nabi, Ali Akbar Khan and Abdul Samad Arshad were among the players who joined the squad ahead of the knockout stages, giving Solano additional options and greater depth.

The impact of their arrival has been evident in Pakistan’s subsequent performances, particularly their defensive organisation and ability to manage difficult moments against Bangladesh.

India coach Naushad Moosa has also acknowledged that Pakistan present a different challenge from the team his side defeated in the group stage, pointing to the arrival of additional players and the tactical adjustments expected for the final.

‘Biggest achievement’

Abdullah acknowledged the importance of the occasion but insisted that the players would not approach the final any differently from their other matches.

Rather than allowing the pressure of a historic opportunity to affect their performance, the defender wants his teammates to remain disciplined, support one another and follow the instructions of the coaching staff.

“It’s a final, a big game, but we have to take it like any other game. Focus on the plan the coach has set for us, help each other out on the pitch and perform as usual. Nothing extra,” Abdullah said.

He admitted that the pressure of competing for a major regional title was unavoidable, particularly given what victory would mean for Pakistan football, but insisted that it would serve as additional motivation.

“Of course, there is pressure to win a final. It’s a big thing for our country, creating history, and it only motivates us to do better,” he added.

Abdullah also described Pakistan’s qualification for the final as a historic achievement, saying a tournament triumph would take the country’s footballing progress to another level.

“On the footballing side, it is the biggest achievement that we’re here in the final, and if we can go all the way, it will be even bigger,” the captain said.

With Pakistan having played a demanding schedule during the tournament, Solano was also asked whether fatigue could become a concern ahead of the final.

The coach dismissed the suggestion, insisting that his players were mentally prepared for the challenge and would not use the schedule as an excuse.

“Nobody is tired, my friend. We all focus. We all have a strong mentality,” he said. “When you play a final, my friends, the last thing you can be is tired. We are ready for fighting. No excuse. We want to give you everything.”

item.title: Zero tolerance for emboldened criminals. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The 30-minute rampage inside Durbin Bangla restaurant in Mohakhali, simply because an individual was asked to wait for a table, is simply unacceptable. That this escalated to assault of the staff, looting cash, ripping out CCTV hard drives, and inflicting up to Tk30 lakh in damages is infuriating.
That very same night, helmeted gunmen opened fire on Anurag Pharmacy on Mohammadpur's Babar Road -- barely 500 metres from a deputy police commissioner's office -- narrowly missing a sales employee’s head following repeated crude bomb blasts and an extortion demand.
Such incidents cannot be taken as isolated aberrations but rather must be seen as symptoms of a growing culture of impunity tightening and of criminals who have been emboldened due to a lack of consequences for their actions.
When armed extortionists can casually shoot up a busy storefront, and entitled thugs can systematically destroy a thriving restaurant in broad daylight without immediate consequences, the message sent to citizens and business owners is chilling: No one is safe, and criminals no longer fear the state.
What is most troubling is the sluggish, reactive posture of law enforcement. Routine assurances that "investigations are underway" are cold comfort to terrorized workers and entrepreneurs watching their livelihoods shattered.
The state cannot afford to turn a blind eye to escalating urban insecurity or treat violent extortion and mob vandalism as routine policing matters. Protecting life, property, and commercial activity is the most basic obligation of the state.
It’s time to enforce an uncompromising, zero-tolerance policy against street thuggery, political muscle-flexing, and armed extortion. Law enforcement too must hold negligent officers accountable for delayed interventions.
Our capital’s residents and businesses deserve a capital governed by the rule of law and not surrendered to the whims of vandals and gunmen.

item.title: Stop making citizens pay. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
To say that Bangladesh’s banking sector is being drowned by non-performing loans (NPLs) would be a laughable understatement at this point.
With the default loan rate hitting a staggering 32.78%, nearly one out of every three taka disbursed across the country's financial system is now non-performing.
Worse still, many analysts are saying what many have long feared: There is virtually zero chance of recovering 80-90% of these toxic assets.
That the overwhelming majority of this crisis is the direct result of operational failures, procedural sabotage, and outright financial crimes should leave every person in this country fuming.
While full-fledged Islamic banks stagger under a 58.9% default rate and state-owned lenders bleed at 43.2%, willful defaulters continue to exploit court injunctions, currently blocking the recovery of Tk 182,419 crore across 845 pending lawsuits to shield stolen public wealth.
It is entirely unacceptable that ordinary depositors, honest entrepreneurs, and taxpayers are continuously forced to absorb the consequences of such gross impunity.
When banks are starved of liquidity by corporate looters, legitimate businesses face suffocating borrowing costs. In addition, our private sector credit growth has collapsed to dismal lows, and savers continue to watch their hard-earned deposits trapped in dysfunctional institutions.
Tackling such a predicament has long been beyond the capacity of banks alone and the government and the central bank must do better. We must end this cycle of opaque half-measures and taxpayer-funded bailouts.
This starts with regular public disclosures on cash recoveries, capital adequacy, and above all, revealing the identities of top willful defaulters. In addition, independent audits and bank-specific resolution frameworks must be enforced without political interference.
Fixing the banking sector cannot mean endlessly penalizing the general public. The state must hold the ones who broke our banks accountable.

item.title: Is it the technology or its owners?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Sixty years ago, the idea of everyone having a video phone in their pocket was the stuff of science fiction.
That people might spend more time on devices doing things other than making actual phone calls would have seemed stranger still, but here we are. A world where fretting about the impact of our own and other peoples’ screen time on society is a more likely choice to make than going without a phone.
As with climate change, individual decisions and consumer choices count enough to make a difference, but most of the actual power to substantively improve regulations and standards rests with politicians and giant global corporations.
In the run-up to the US mid-term Congressional elections this month, Silicon Valley companies and their owners donated $600 million dollars to Republican candidates.
A large proportion of this came from Elon Musk spending about $200m on supporting Ken Paxton, the losing Republican candidate for a Senate seat in Texas.
Whilst the vast amounts given to Republican candidates did not prevent an anti-Trump wave of Democratic party successes, they reflect the growing amounts being spent by Silicon Valley titans on buying political influence.
Big Tech’s societal and environmental footprint and its record of abusing monopolistic positions, aggressively minimizing paying taxes, failing to safeguard privacy, and designing algorithms to addict users and profit from amplifying political extremes and other harmful content already raises many ethical questions. Yet, the latest spending added to the concerns about its political lobbying and future trajectory.
Moore’s law, named after a co-founder of Intel, observed that the number of transistors it is technically possible to fit onto an integrated circuit can be doubled every two years at little increase in cost. For decades it was this rate of exponential improvement that enabled ever more computing power to be made available at lower prices to ordinary consumers.
In turn, these underpinned bigger projections and valuations for the sector. In 2016, the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization was Apple with the aggregate value of its shares peaking above $500bn.
Ten years on, its value is ten times larger at $5 trillion. This is different from being the world’s largest company by actual revenue; Apple’s revenues place it as only the seventh largest company.
Apple’s stock market value reflects the willingness of investors to bet on the tech sector’s future growth. Since 2020 this optimism has become based less on Moore’s law delivering cost reductions for consumers -- its effect is slowing down as semiconductor manufacturers adjust to the growing complexity and cost of making ever smaller circuits just as global supply chains have fragmented -- and more on a belief in future profits from AI.
Potential impacts of AI, both positive and negative, are easy enough to imagine, given the pace of change the sector is promising. Predictions of technological dystopias and utopias are a hardy staple of speculative fiction.
Right now, AI has an insatiable appetite for capital investment in scaling up computational power and data centres. These are demanding ever greater amounts of electricity and water for cooling systems.
The cost neutral arithmetic of energy costs remaining stable as computer chips and systems become smaller and more powerful promised by Moore’s law has been turned completely upside down by a globalized gold rush to grow AI.
Even in a world that had free energy, this direction of travel would be controversial given the sector’s impact on jobs, but in a world with a growing population seeking to cut carbon emissions, amid plenty of pre-existing concerns about Big Tech, it is politically toxic.
Seen in this light, the sectors’ growing political donations and lobbying efforts on AI, not just in the United States, but in countries around the world, are easy to explain.
Like other industries, it wants to keep pipelines of investment flowing and persuade politicians to support them with financial incentives and favourable laws.
But what if it is all just snake oil and a digital Ponzi scheme?
Scepticism is a rational stance given the vast scope and impact of the IT sector. But even where politicians seek to regulate aspects of the sector, their actions tend to be limited or seem like locking a stable door after the horse has bolted.
Given that parts of the sector like digital cryptocurrencies were designed to be largely decentralized and unregulated in nature, such naivete is troubling given that aspects of it can be used to enable criminality.
Dogmatic faith in future growth and cultish attitudes towards IT founders and products abound around the sector and among many consumers. Perhaps not surprisingly, many of the biggest critics of the ownership structures and strategies of the sector come from within its highly educated workforce and support the open-source movement.
Of course, the argument that technology is simply a tool that can be used for good or bad is ostensibly an objective one.
But when those making it are tech giants with monopolistic tendencies that stand to profit either way, calls for democratic scrutiny, breaking up monopolies, public accountability, and for that matter public ownership, all deserve to be heard.
It’s the oligarchs, stupid.
Niaz Alam is London Bureau Chief, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Calling out the digital inquisitors. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In the interconnected landscape of modern South Asia, the digital square was once heralded as a beacon of democratic expression. Today, however, it increasingly resembles a medieval plaza where a baying mob gathers, stones in hand, waiting for the next target to be dragged into the light.
Across India, Pakistan, and the wider region, whenever tragedy strikes or a viral controversy erupts, a familiar and sickening ritual unfolds online. Behind a shroud of anonymous handles, inactive profile pictures, and automated bot networks, a pervasive strain of digital chauvinism rears its head.
These faceless commentators rush with predatory speed to demean, judge, and ultimately blame women for their own suffering.
Whether it is a high-profile criminal case of rape and murder, a domestic abuse tragedy, or a viral public misstep, the verdict from this digital jury is always preemptive and predictable: The woman is guilty.
This phenomenon is not merely an annoyance of modern internet culture; it is a profound social rot.
It reveals a deep-seated, short-sighted misogyny that weaponizes human suffering to reinforce archaic prejudices, demanding that we confront and socially shun these insidious behaviours before they erode the moral fabric of our societies.
The anatomy of victim-blaming
The most harrowing manifestation of this online malice occurs in the wake of heinous crimes -- rapes, assaults, and murders that shock the public conscience.
In a just society, a horrific crime against a woman should provoke universal outrage, sorrow, and an uncompromising demand for justice against the perpetrator.
Yet, in the virtual echo chambers of South Asia, the narrative is routinely subverted.
When a woman is attacked or killed, the digital inquisitors immediately pivot away from the perpetrator’s guilt to dissect the victim’s life with microscopic scrutiny.
Why was she out alone at night? Where was her male guardian or family member? What was she wearing?
In cases involving minors, the depravity sinks even lower, with commentators bizarrely projecting adult anxieties onto children, questioning their clothing or presence in public spaces as if to rationalize the unrationalizable.
This is the quintessence of victim-blaming. It is a psychological defense mechanism rooted in a fragile worldview that cannot bear the thought of a chaotic, dangerous world where women are independent agents.
By blaming the victim, these commentators construct a comforting illusion of control: “If she hadn’t done X, Y, or Z, she would have been safe.”
In doing so, they absolve the actual criminal and place the burden of virtue and safety entirely on the shoulders of women.
It sends a chilling message to half the population: Your safety is conditional, and if you step outside the narrow parameters dictated by society, your tragedy is your own fault.
Attire, liberty, and the ‘liberal mind’
Beyond violent crimes, everyday viral controversies draw the same predatory swarm.
Let a video surface of a woman making a mistake in public, navigating a personal dispute, or simply living her life on her own terms, and the social media comment sections transform into cesspools of moral panic.
Here, the faceless profiles deploy a standard checklist of grievances.
Every complex socio-economic issue, every cultural shift, and every personal failure is summarily blamed on "indecent attire," "polygamous behaviour" (often invoked as a catch-all insult), and the dreaded "liberal mind."
If a woman exercises agency over her life, her career, or her relationships, she is immediately branded as a corrupting influence on traditional values.
The underlying rhetoric is transparently hypocritical: Men can indulge in every conceivable excess without denting their moral standing, but a woman’s entire character is judged by a single snapshot, a rumour, or a manipulated video clip.
Commentators jump on these bandwagons without a second thought for context, nuance, or basic human empathy.
Facts do not matter to the mob. Once the narrative is set -- that women have become too "modern," too "independent," and too "uncontrolled" -- the digital machinery of character assassination goes into overdrive.
From faceless bots to female envy
What makes this digital ecosystem particularly toxic is its composition.
It is propelled not just by men hiding behind pseudonyms, but also by a distinct psychological undercurrent of internalized misogyny.
On one hand, we have the legions of nameless male profiles -- the virtual moral police whose own lives are often defined by frustration, stagnation, and a deep-seated insecurity regarding modern, autonomous women.
Their online vitriol is an outlet for impotent rage against a changing world where women refuse to remain silent, subservient second-class citizens.
Protected by the anonymity of a screen, these men project their anxieties onto viral targets, seeking a toxic sense of community and validation from other like-minded misogynists.
On the other hand, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: This phenomenon is not exclusively male.
Often, women themselves participate in the shaming, driven by a potent mix of social conditioning and deep-seated envy. In societies where female worth has historically been tied to strict conformity, seeing another woman break the mold can trigger a defensive reaction.
Some women, having internalized patriarchal standards to survive, view independent or non-conformist women as a threat to the fragile security they have carved out for themselves.
By joining the mob, they signal their own "purity" and conformity. This betrayal from within is perhaps the most tragic aspect of the cycle, as it fractures solidarity precisely when it is needed most.
Call for social ostracization
We have reached a critical juncture in the digital evolution of South Asia. The line between online commentary and real-world harm has long since blurred.
When internet trolls normalize victim-blaming, they create a cultural climate where violence against women is minimized, excused, or implicitly encouraged.
This behaviour cannot simply be brushed aside as "just internet noise" or the ramblings of "trolls being trolls."
These voices shape public perception, intimidate survivors into silence, and deter women from seeking justice or participating fully in public life.
Combating this requires a fundamental cultural reset.
We must strip away the digital armour that emboldens these cowards.
Anonymity on social media should no longer be a free pass to terrorize victims of crime or ruin reputations with impunity.
Platforms must be held accountable for enabling networks of abuse and algorithmic amplification of misogyny.
More importantly, the remedy must come from society itself.
These shamelessly insensitive remarks and baseless accusations must be actively confronted and socially shunned.
Just as we would condemn someone for making excuses for a thief or a murderer in a physical room, we must call out those who excuse abuse and degradation in the digital room.
Friends, family members, colleagues, and community leaders must make it clear that victim-blaming and casual misogyny are not "opinions" to be debated -- they are moral failures.
Until the cost of participating in online harassment becomes too high -- until social circles, workplaces, and public platforms make it socially untenable to bully and blame women -- the digital public square will remain a dangerous frontier.
It is time to drag these faceless inquisitors out of the shadows and hold them to the light of accountability.
Women in our society deserve nothing less than a culture that protects their dignity, respects their autonomy, and refuses to negotiate with the malice of the mob.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: One blood, many names. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
I read Ziauddin Choudhury’s Understanding the Modern Bangladeshi with the quiet gratitude one feels on hearing a stranger describe the inside of one’s own chest.
He traces, with a civil servant’s clarity, the long road by which a people learned to stop choosing: The rival answers to colonial India’s question -- the line that ran from Sir Syed to the Muslim League, minority and safeguards, against Bengal’s own instinct, which found identity in a language and a soil as much as in a faith.
He walks us through 1952, when “we are Muslims in Pakistan” quietly became “we are Bengalis whose tongue is our nationhood” and through 1971, which turned sentiment into a state.
He reads Article 12 of the 1972 Constitution as it was meant to be read -- not as an assault on religion, but as an assault on the use of religion as the ticket to power and citizenship. He ends, rightly, on Tagore and Nazrul. I would not change a word of it. I want only to sit beside him and add what a man sees from inside the thing he describes.
I am old enough to remember a Bangladesh that no constitution could legislate. In the first years after independence, in the lanes where I grew up, a friend had no religion. I do not mean we were tolerant of one another’s faiths; I mean the question did not arise.
I could not have told you, of half the boys I played with, whether their mothers turned toward Mecca or lit a lamp before an image -- it was not a thing one knew, because it was not a thing that mattered.
That society was real. I did not dream it. And the slow tearing of that fabric, thread by thread, in the decades since, is a wound those of us who remember carry still. I write, in part, to describe the wholeness before it is forgotten by those too young to have stood in it.
For I was born beside a Bengali river, into a family that would be called Hindu, though I have never once been able to feel the border that word is meant to draw around me. I am not a theologian. I am, if anything, a civilizational Sanatani -- heir to an old subcontinental inheritance the way a Florentine is heir to the Renaissance, not by doctrine but by blood and weather and song.
My DNA is the DNA of the subcontinent, which is to say it is Hindu and Muslim and Buddhist and a dozen older things at once, and it has never asked me to choose. So when Ziauddin Choudhury writes that being Bengali and being Muslim need not negate each other, I do not read it as a Muslim’s reassurance. I read it as the description of my own body.
And let me grant, plainly, what a man with my name is not always expected to grant. Some time ago I sat reading the old constitutional quarrel of the 1930s -- Jinnah insisting that the Muslims of India needed a voice of their own, one the Hindu majority could not simply overrule; Nehru, the secular, unable to see how faith could enter a question of constituencies at all. It was an all-India argument, about Hindus and Muslims in the abstract; neither man had Bengal in his thoughts, and the word Bengali appears nowhere in it. But as I read, my mind slipped homeward, to my own soil, and a sentence rose in me -- not a proverb, nothing I had been taught, only my own voice murmuring what I suddenly understood: Musolmanra to jole bheshe aseni -- the Muslims did not come floating down the river.
The Bengali Muslim is no stranger washed in from elsewhere. Some came to Islam by conversion and many did not; but all of them rose from this very soil, the same villages, and the same rivers that gave me my grandfathers.
The Bengali Muslim and the Bengali Hindu are not two peoples who learned to share a country. They are one people wearing two of its names. This is not a poet’s flourish: Their belonging is not a courtesy I extend, but a fact older than any objection could be.
Let me give the synthesis a face, from the side Choudhury was too modest to claim. In the house where I grew up, the morning did not begin with a clock. It began with the Azan from the mosque down the lane, and it was by that call -- a Muslim call, in a Hindu household -- that my mother knew the hour to wake her son for his studies.
No one found this strange. The Azan was not another faith intruding; it was the sound of morning itself, the texture of a shared Bengali dawn. We were not tolerated guests at the edge of the nation. We were the nation, in one of its oldest forms.
Let me confess something that may surprise anyone who reads only the name at the top of this essay. I do not pray to Durga. And yet few sights give me more joy than a Bengali home at Diwali -- the rows of small lamps along the windowsills and the rooftops, the whole simple, childlike happiness of a festival of light that now glows from Dhaka to Kolkata to New York.
The only thing that moves me as much is the sight of children in their new clothes on Eid morning, shining with a pride they can barely hold in. I love both the same, and for the same reason.
To me, neither is theology; both are culture -- the way a people’s faith flowers into everyday life -- and such culture is among the most beautiful things human beings have ever made. A man who can be stirred by the Azan, light a lamp at Diwali, and smile at an Eid procession has not lost his religion. He has understood what religion was for.
This is why the minority is not a footnote to the story of modern Bangladesh. It is the proof of the story. A secularism that forbids religion from deciding citizenship is only as true as its weakest-placed citizen.
Choudhury notes, almost in passing, the great Hindu departure from East Bengal, and maps the longing for undivided Bengal onto the Hindus of the western shore -- those who left. But the leaving and the staying were often one family, not two.
My own parents and grandparents did not go. Yet most of my kin did -- nearly all of my mother’s people, nearly all of the family I married into -- packing in a single season what it had taken generations to root.
So I do not write as one who stayed, gazing across at those who left. I write from the torn seam itself, where half a household remained and half became a memory on the far side of a line.
For those of us on the staying side, East Bengal is not the recollection of a lost ancestral home across a border. It is home -- and we are what remains of the synthesis here, keeping it because someone must.
In the summer of 2024 and the months that followed, temples were burned and homes were marked; and last month -- in an image I cannot forget -- a mural of Rabindranath Tagore in Dhaka was defaced, blackened, as if the Bishwakobi himself, the first of all Asia to win the Nobel, could be painted out of the place that raised him.
When a mob blackens Tagore, it is not a Hindu who is attacked. It is the synthesis. It is the very thing Choudhury spent his essay defending. For Tagore belongs to no sect; he belongs to the morning, like the Azan.
And here the oldest lesson returns to warn us. A people cannot bury their language in the grave of their faith; when they are forced to, the nation tears. East Pakistan was Muslim -- as Muslim as the West -- and it tore anyway -- first in spirit, in 1952, when its students died for their mother tongue, and then in body, in 1971 -- because identity is never one thread, and you cannot pull out the thread of language in the name of the thread of religion without the whole cloth coming apart in your hands.
That is not a Hindu’s grievance nor a Muslim’s. It is simply what our history taught us. We learned it once, against an imposed tongue. We must not now unlearn it against one another.
Consider Nazrul, whom Choudhury rightly names in the same breath as Tagore. Our rebel poet wrote hamds and naats to the Prophet with one hand and shyama sangeet to the goddess Kali with the other; he married across the very line that was meant to be uncrossable, and raised children who carried both inheritances in their names.
Nazrul was not a Muslim poet who dabbled, nor a secular poet who hedged. He was the non-divide itself, walking around in a single body, singing. If we wish to know what the modern Bangladeshi could be, we need no constitutional theory. We need only read him.
I am not writing as a Hindu, pleading a Hindu’s case. I am writing for everyone this ancient and exhausting divide has ever wounded -- the Muslim woman told her Bengali songs are un-Islamic; the Hindu shopkeeper watching his shutter; the Buddhist in the Chittagong Hills, the Christian in the north; and the Bengali Muslim majority too, robbed of something each time a zealot insists their faith can be purchased only at the price of their culture.
The wound has no religion. That is the whole point. It cuts through one body -- ours -- and the blood that runs from it is one blood, whatever name we give it.
Choudhury ends on a hope: A Bangladesh where one may love Tagore, keep Pohela Baishakh, and hold Islam close, with no identity forced to negate another. I share that hope entirely.
I would only extend it by a single clause. The synthesis is complete not when no Bengali must choose between being Bengali and being Muslim -- that is already won, and Choudhury has shown us how.
It is complete when no Bengali must disappear to let another feel whole. A nation does not prove its secularism by the comfort of its majority. It proves it at the temple that is not burned, the mural that is not blackened, the neighbour whose morning prayer -- to whatever name, in whatever tongue -- is simply allowed to be the sound of the street.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, Sweden, where he has practised medicine for a lifetime, and where, on winter mornings, he sometimes still wakes up expecting an Azan that is five thousand kilometres away.

item.title: Holding the NBR accountable. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) latest push to develop a specialized app to collect a 0.2% advance tax -- deducting Tk2 per thousand on goods supplied via distributors starting next January is yet another display of the National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) reactive decision making.
While bringing informal businesses into the formal tax net and digitizing transactions are sound principles in theory, the timing and execution of this move expose a deeply flawed administrative mindset.
That NBR is already facing a staggering revenue shortfall exceeding Tk50,000 crore in just the first four months of FY27 brings to light all we need to know about the institution’s inability to set realistic targets.
Moreover, the tax authority is once again taking the path of least resistance: Potentially squeezing small, vulnerable shopkeepers because it lacks the competence and political will to collect from the wealthy elite.
For years, the NBR and the Ministry of Finance have indulged in the annual farce of setting wildly unrealistic, inflated revenue targets disconnected from ground realities. When those projections inevitably collapse, the agency panics and unleashes predatory compliance burdens on the smallest economic actors.
Instead of dismantling entrenched tax evasion among the powerful and wealthy, be they corporate conglomerates or individuals, they continue targeting individual middle class employees and the millions of small retail traders who are already battling sluggish sales and relentless inflation.
Expecting a corner shop owner to maintain five separate VAT registers, hire accountants, and absorb advance tax deductions is administrative harassment disguised as reform. Inevitably, these compounding compliance costs then get passed directly onto struggling consumers through higher retail prices.
It is unacceptable that taxpayers continue to pay the price for chronic regulatory incompetence without any repercussions for the officials responsible for perpetual revenue failures.
If we want true fiscal reform, then we must be setting realistic targets, automating collection from high-income tax evaders, and holding NBR leadership accountable for its systemic collection failures every year.

item.title: Paving the way for women to lead. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We agree with Speaker Major (retd) Hafiz Uddin Ahmed that giving women the opportunity to win 100 parliamentary seats through direct elections, rather than confining them to the existing reserved-seat system, is the way forward if we care about genuine political empowerment of women.
As this newspaper noted in our previous editorial, "Where are the women leaders?," Bangladesh's democratic landscape suffers from a staggering deficit of female decision-makers. That in the 2026 parliamentary election, women secured a dismal seven general seats is simply unacceptable, and that more is not being done to rectify this glaring issue is a failure of the state.
The message is unmistakable: While women stand at the vanguard of street movements and grassroots campaigns, patriarchal party structures systematically lock them out when power is distributed.
For far too long, the reserved-seat mechanism has been used by major political parties as a convenient smokescreen to avoid nominating women for general constituencies. This must end.
Appointed rather than elected, reserved-seat lawmakers frequently lack direct constituency authority and are treated as secondary actors in legislative chambers.
Moving toward 100 directly elected seats for women would shatter this patronizing status quo, legitimizing female leaders through popular mandates and giving them undeniable political weight.
Empowering half the population is not merely a matter of social justice but an absolute prerequisite for national development, especially at a time when regressive beliefs threaten to infiltrate our politics.
No nation, and certainly not ours, can hope to build a resilient, modern economy while sidelining the talent, perspective, and leadership of 50% of its citizens.
We need the government, and by extension the leaders of all political parties, to move swiftly from rhetorical endorsement to constitutional and electoral reform.
Dismantling tokenism and establishing direct electoral pathways for women is an obvious, non-negotiable step forward. It is time to stop treating female representation as political charity and let women claim their rightful place as equal architects of our future.

What empty malls can teach us about getting richer. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
How new technology makes us all richer can be a little difficult to work through. We can all see -- because it's obvious -- how rich the entrepreneurs who own the new technology get.
Jeff Bezos, for example, has a second yacht to carry his helicopter while following his first yacht. Which is, you know, pretty rich. Mark Zuckerberg has half a Hawaiian island and Ellison, of Oracle, has most of another -- both also have large yachts.
But what do we get out of this arrangement? One of the reasons populist politicians gain so much attraction from voters is that tracking that down can be difficult. There are answers. Zuckerberg's fortune comes from, in part, us getting free telephone calls on WhatsApp and Facebook Messenger. OK, free phone calls may or may not be of huge value to us individually but there are 4 billion of us -- half the entire world -- who get them which does add up.
The very existence of Amazon has cut 0.1 to 0.2% off the US inflation rate for two decades now. Just that price competition from it has lowered all prices for everyone by 2-4% on everything they buy. That's worth one yacht, maybe two.
We can also look at this in more detail in Bangladesh. Owners of shopping malls in Dhaka are selling up. Because they cannot make money any more and the reason is : “The rise of online retail,” “shop online,” the “expansion of e-commerce,” and so on.
We see this in my native Britain as well. The Office for National Statistics records that online sales are 28% of total retail sales today -- up from 3% in 2006. As a result, we simply require fewer shops and it's true that retail landlords are suffering. At least one of the large companies -- Intu -- went bust some years back as a result.
This doesn't mean that no one ever wants to go to the shops and everyone wants to only buy online. There really are those who enjoy going shopping just for the joy of going shopping.
What we're therefore seeing in some other countries is a division in the shopping experience. Yes, we still have little local shops where we can get little supplies of necessities -- a gallon of milk, a loaf of bread. We also have the big shopping experiences of places where it's possible to go and have a day out having that active fun of shopping.
The places feeling the financial pressure are those that used to provide the shopping that had to be done and that few find that fun. That's now better -- or preferentially -- done by point, click, and the delivery van.
These things are all true but we do tend to not put as much emphasis on these benefits to us -- even as they clearly are benefits because this is why we do things -- as we do upon the problems of those going bust because we've changed our ways.
We also tend not to feel a 1 or 2% change in price levels, or any other gradual change, over years. Even as they are how we get richer over time. One and two percent really does add up over decades.
Then along comes an economist and points out that this isn't, not really, how we all get richer. The real point is this: “As a result, the owners decided to sell off the property. Discussions are currently underway with several entities, including hospitals, corporate firms, and banks.”
Dhaka has a limited amount of land. As the most densely populated city on the planet, it has a very limited amount of land. So, if we stop using land for one purpose, then we get empty land that can then be used for another.
We're made richer by whatever value we put upon having a hospital, more jobs and employment from corporations, or even a bank -- hopefully one that doesn't lose all the money.
And that is how economists say we get richer. This new way of doing things, this new technology, uses fewer resources -- less land here, but it can be less labour, less energy, etc -- and this means we've now newly freed up resources to go and produce something else that we want.
We are richer by whatever value we put on this new thing that it is now possible to produce for our enjoyment. OK, hospitals aren't really about enjoyment other than in the leaving of them alive. But you get the point.
Economists are indeed strange people, but they really do say that we get richer when we stop using resources. Because when we don't use something in limited supply to do this thing, here, that then frees up the supply of that thing to be used to do something else. We are richer by the value we place on that new thing being done.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: The growing threat of fake photocards. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A teenager’s body hangs from the Shaheed Minar in Manikganj. Beside it sits the portrait of an SSC examinee named Shihab, under a headline styled like Samakal’s: He scored a golden GPA-5 two days after his death. The photocard adds one more detail. It says the boy belonged to the Chhatra League.
FactWatch investigated this photocard in August 2026 and rated it false. Two different boys who shared a name had been merged into one story. Samakal’s real report was about a different Shihab. A dead child, a party label, and a trusted masthead: That mix is built to make people angry before they think.
Not a fluke, but a format
Between September 2025 and February 2026, fact-checkers debunked 690 distinct fake photocards. Nearly half of them were political misinformation.
Five simple elements are being used:
Prof Sumon Rahman, Head of the Media Studies and Journalism Department, ULAB, says the photocards are easy to produce and seem to carry a newsroom’s endorsement.
FactWatch’s 2021 review already found visuals and videos were the favourite carriers of falsehood. Rumor Scanner logged 105 fake photocards in 2023, then 324 cases in just nine months of 2024.
FactWatch spent the 10 weeks around Bangladesh’s 13th parliamentary election tracking exactly this. Between December 11, 2025 and February 17, 2026, its researchers logged and verified 94 distinct disinformation cases tied to the vote.
The breakdown is the interesting part: AI-generated content 16%, doctored excerpts 6%, and fake media photocards, the branded ones mimicking a specific outlet’s logo and layout, at 21%.
Made for big moments
Photocards follow the news cycle. Volumes spiked right after each major political event. After Osman Hadi was shot in December 2025, photocards about laundered money and invented quotes multiplied. When Tarique Rahman returned on December 25, others claimed patients were dying in ambulances.
The pattern predates that vote. During talk of Dr Yunus resigning in May 2025, 56% of that episode’s misinformation used fake photocards. Even a local union parishad race in Pirojpur drew fake photocards. Amar Desh’s design was copied the most, followed by Kaler Kantho, Jamuna Television, RTV, and Kalbela.
What is trending now
Artificial intelligence is the newest layer. FactWatch debunked an August 2026 card attributed to the power minister, and its detection tools suggested it was AI-generated. One study found 28% of AI cases were AI-edited photocards carrying false quotes.
Two other trends are more concerning. Photocards have turned sexual: Researchers counted 34 degrading cases, including a fake gang-rape claim about Dr Mahmuda Mitu . They stoke communal fear, such as invented threats to Hindu households over which symbol they vote for.
Who makes them, and why
Dismislab traced photocards to partisan pages across the spectrum. Roughly 62% attacked parties, 16% targeted individuals, and 12.5% puffed up popularity. A polls-day review found pro-Jamaat networks especially active, while Rumour Scanner says Indian accounts and local pages both feed wider campaigns against Bangladesh.
Spoof pages do the heavy lifting. FactWatch found that fake Amar Desh photocards spread from a look-alike page with about 14,000 followers, not the newspaper’s official one.
During the election period, multiple media outlets -- including Kaler Kantho, DBC News, Jamuna TV, Channel24, Jugantor, Amar Desh, BBC Bangla, and Prothom Alo -- had their identities spoofed, creating a network too expansive for any individual newsroom to track.
The readers who pay
A photocard is built for a thumb and a hurry, which suits newcomers. One national survey found 53% of adults are online, half for under five years, and about 40% of users are unfamiliar with search engines.
Unicef’s study found news literacy very low among people without high-school education. One analyst calls the problem a threat to a digitally illiterate population.
In an interview study of 29 Bangladeshi users, lower-education participants leaned on people. A driver said that if his boss shares something, he assumes it is credible. A housewife re-shares her sister’s posts because the sister is a government official. A retired man asks his granddaughter before he shares.
Now picture a photocard landing in that chain. It carries a familiar logo, so the outlet vouches for it. It comes from a cousin or a neighbour, so the family vouches for it. Two layers of borrowed trust arrive before anyone has read a word.
A Bangladesh misinformation primer notes that in some rural areas, people know Facebook but not the wider internet. Messaging apps like Imo, popular among migrant workers, carry rumours without any editor in the loop. A photocard that would take a scroll to debunk online can travel through a bazaar as paper. Nobody in that crowd opens a fact-checker’s page.
It also assumes the outlet’s page is easy to find. Outlets already post clarification notices, but they reach only the page followers.
When fake photocards multiply, the honest ones lose value. Readers learn that a logo proves nothing, and then they start to suspect real reporting too. Amar Desh’s editor warned that people begin to think the paper publishes fake news.
There is a cruel twist. A person caught out by one fake photocard often decides all photocards are fake. Disbelief becomes as useful to manipulators as belief. He may think the media is dying too. I worry now that a real piece of news can just be waved away as “just a photocard.”
Zulker Naeen is a research coordinator, Center for Critical and Qualitative Studies, and adjunct faculty, Department of Media Studies and Journalism, University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh.

item.title: Abdul Samad’s late strike sends Pakistan into historic SAFF Championship final. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Abdul Samad Arshad struck a sensational late winner to guide Pakistan into their first-ever SAFF Championship final, as Nolberto Solano’s side held off sustained pressure from hosts Bangladesh to secure a dramatic 1-0 semi-final victory at the National Stadium on Saturday.

With Bangladesh dominating possession and looking the more likely side to break the deadlock, Samad produced a moment of individual brilliance in the closing stages to silence the home crowd and make history for Pakistan football.

The Denmark-based forward collected the ball on the right, skilfully shifted it between his feet to create space before unleashing a powerful left-footed drive that beat goalkeeper Mehedi Hasan Srabon with around five minutes of regulation time remaining.

The victory marks another significant milestone in a remarkable year for Pakistan football, with the national side now just one win away from claiming its first regional title.

Bangladesh enjoyed around 62-64 per cent possession and looked to make the most of home advantage, but Pakistan remained disciplined and organised defensively, frustrating the hosts while posing a threat on the counter-attack. Despite having considerably less of the ball, the visitors registered more shots and efforts on target.

Bangladesh, who had topped Group ‘A’ unbeaten with victories over Bhutan and Sri Lanka, pressed for an equaliser in the closing minutes.

Frustrated home supporters even threw a flare onto the pitch, briefly interrupting play, but Pakistan held firm to secure a famous victory.

The result also ends a long history of semi-final disappointment for the Shaheens, who had reached the last four on four previous occasions without managing to progress to the final.

Solano’s men had reached the semi-finals as Group ‘B’ runners-up after opening their campaign with a 3-2 defeat to India, despite a spirited late fightback, before responding with a convincing 3-0 victory over the Maldives.

The arrival of several overseas-based players, including Samad, for the knockout rounds provided a timely boost, with the group-stage fixtures having fallen outside the FIFA international window.

Pakistan will now face arch-rivals and defending champions India in Tuesday’s final after the latter defeated Bhutan 2-1 in the other semi-final.

Solano’s side will be aiming to cap their historic campaign by overcoming India and securing Pakistan’s first-ever SAFF Championship title.

NCCIA warns youth against joining illegal call centres for lucrative salaries. [ dawn ]
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) on Saturday warned that loopholes in the existing system are being exploited by illegal call centres, online betting operators and international fraud networks to launder money and trap victims.

Addressing a press conference, NCCIA (Islamabad/Rawalpindi) Additional Director Muhammad Shoaib Khan said fake companies were being registered with weak verification, after which bank accounts opened in their names were integrated with loan apps, betting and gaming portals to receive and transfer illicit funds.

Therefore, he called for stricter rules on company registration and bank account verification.

The press conference was primarily called to warn educated youths against becoming involved in cybercrime by joining illegal call centres in pursuit of lucrative salaries, urging those seeking jobs with call centres to ask their employers where they are registered and appealing to parents to check whether their children were working at an illegal call centre carrying out scams, fraud or other illicit activities.

“Ask them what documents the company has, what registration it operates under, which company they work for, which company is providing the loans, where the money is coming from and who is putting money into these applications,” Khan said.

Acknowledging that young people and university students were engaging in such jobs because the salaries were higher than average, he noted that they risked ending up becoming part of the entire trap and operation.

“If your son or daughter is arrested in such an operation, the FIR (first information report) becomes part of their record. Tomorrow, when they need a character certificate or apply for a government job, that record can affect them,” the NCCIA officer warned.

He said the issue concerns merchant accounts provided by banks and the accounts into which money is deposited. A bank account is linked to a company that may already have been registered despite weaknesses in proper verification, standard operating procedures or the Know Your Customer (KYC) process.

“After the company has been registered, the bank opens an account for it. The operators then take that company’s bank account and integrate it with their online betting or gaming portal,” Khan said, adding that the NCCIA team is working on recommendations to these institutions so that they improve their checking systems.

The additional director said the agency already raised the issue with senior officials at the policy level, and loopholes identified during investigations and interrogations are brought to light so they can be addressed.

He said the NCCIA wants to address cases where one-person companies or similar companies were registered and their bank accounts were subsequently used in this way.

Meanwhile, Khan said that the NCCIA identified the role and other details of each individual involved: who used which computer, what their role was, the extent of their involvement, who trapped victims, made the calls and edited the material.

“We do not treat everyone as having played the same role. After establishing those roles, we prepare the proper FIR and proceed accordingly,” he explained.

The NCCIA additional director noted the agency raided two call centres in the Islamabad-Rawalpindi Zone over the past three days.

In the Rawalpindi raid, 11 people, including 10 women, were arrested, while in the Islamabad raid, 143 people were arrested, including 43 women. He said the centres were carrying out transnational scams and fraud, targeting countries in South Asia.

Modus operandi

Explaining the modus operandi, he said the two centres in the latest raids worked differently.

At the Rawalpindi centre, an elaborate setup posing as the police had been created. The operators would offer loans, and when it was time to recover the loans — or when they had trapped someone and wanted to extract money — they would call and scam that victim.

The suspects would tell a person that they were either being surveilled or on a hit list. Once someone fell into their trap, they would transfer the person to a setup made to look like the police in Bangladesh, put the victim in contact with someone posing as a police officer and then extort money.

At the Islamabad centre, they worked in layers; first, they trapped the victim and convinced them to install an application on their mobile phone. Once it was installed, they obtained access to the person’s photo gallery.

After accessing the gallery and obtaining a selfie, they would issue a loan for a minimal amount. But their real target was to collect the person’s credentials: mobile number, personal information and other data.

They also obtained information about close family members whom the borrower had identified as guarantors, such as a wife, father, brother, cousin or other family members named as next of kin.

Once they had collected all these credentials, the case would be passed to senior members. When they had extracted all of the money they could from someone, they would wipe out that person’s account and close the case.

The second method was to take a person’s selfie and other pictures from their phone gallery and edit them into pornographic material, using the person’s face in what appeared to be a professional manner. They would then start threatening, harassing and blackmailing the victim.

“Even though the resulting pictures might have been fabricated, the threats were still effective. The victim would be under tremendous pressure, fearing that the images would reach their community or family. Under that pressure, the person would start paying money,” Khan said.

He said the scammers extracted personal information in the name of loans, manipulated it and used it against the victims, or created sexual content depicting the victim and extracted money through harassment and blackmail.

Responding to a question about alleged masterminds, Khan said they were present at every call centre and also arrested. After that, the agency would investigate local facilitators, including whoever rented out the building, those who made the arrangements and connections and those who set up the operation through a fake company.

“We also trace the people who pay the bills and pursue those involved. Then we work at the transnational and international level. We have liaison arrangements with different countries. If a handler or operator belongs to another country, we communicate through embassies and our international contacts,” he noted.

A global problem

The additional director further stated that international cooperation was being strengthened because such call centres had become a global problem.

The NCCIA would handle investigations in Pakistan, while the relevant agencies in the United Kingdom, the United States, China and other countries would handle such matters in their respective jurisdictions.

Khan added that in a previous Rawalpindi call centre case, foreign nationals were arrested and are in jail, and will face trial according to Pakistani law.

On the changing methods of call centres, he acknowledged that they were no longer necessarily operating in large plazas. In one house, 10 to 12 people gathered with a computer setup and connected their applications and websites to bank accounts.

Someone may be sitting in another country while the people here trap the victim, the NCCIA official pointed out. Once the victim starts depositing money into the account, the person in the other country receives the money.

He noted that the Rawalpindi centre had been operating for about a month, while the Islamabad facility had been established only 15 or 20 days earlier. The floor managers and overall HR managers at both centres were locals, he added.

“We will investigate and interrogate further to establish who is connected to the back-end operation. We need to find out in which country the application was developed, who developed it and who is handling it,” Khan stated.

Staying safe

Speaking about how the youth could tell which call centres are legal, Khan said the first thing is common understanding.

“If an entire floor is generating sexual content, you know that is illegal. That is a matter of common sense.”

Khan added that when applying for a job, young people should ask which organisation the business is registered with, who approved it and what approval it received from the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan.

Moreover, he said many loan applications were operating legally because they have proper permission and follow a lawful procedure. The NCCIA inspects their whole system, including whether the applications are accessing people’s photo galleries, and examines their loan-recovery mechanism. If a borrower does not pay, there are legal channels and procedures for recovery.

On foreign nationals allegedly involved in cybercrime, Khan said he did not have an exact number, but acknowledged that there have been many deportations.

“The number in prison is in the hundreds. When the agency raids one call centre alone, it may find between 150 and 250 people on average,” he added.

Khan also rejected attributing call-centre crime to one nationality, saying there are people of multiple nationalities who come to Pakistan and become involved in this work.

The agency had also arrested 37 suspects allegedly involved in harassment and blackmail cases over the past two to three years, the official added. The suspects had extracted money from women through harassment and blackmail, and the victims had endured this for the past two or three years.

On online betting and gambling, Khan said operators initially give users profits deliberately, enticing people to put more money into these portals. They then assess the victim’s financial capacity and, once convinced that the victim has invested their savings, they wipe out the money and cut off contact.

“We are working on this issue and, God willing, will take further action soon. We are making every effort to address fraud involving millions and billions in the name of online betting and gaming,” he stressed.

Appealing to young people and businesspeople, including major business owners, Khan urged them against putting business money into buying tokens online and depositing money into gaming applications, gaming websites or betting platforms.

“Initially, they may even be allowed to withdraw their money, but essentially the operators are giving them time, playing with their mind and encouraging them to keep depositing more money,” he explained.

Khan said the cyber-patrolling teams work around the clock, 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

item.title: The miracle cure in your Facebook feed is killing Bangladeshis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every Bangladeshi family knows the scene. My father is newly diagnosed with diabetes. The doctor's advice is the same as always: Medication, diet, regular monitoring, lifelong discipline. It is sound advice, and it is exhausting to follow.
Then his morning walk friend forwards a video to him. A man in a white coat promises a cure in seven days, with no injections and no side effects, for only Tk3,500 and cash on delivery.
This is not harmless chatter. It is a business, and its customers are dying.
Diabetes is a lifelong condition for which no cure currently exists. That inconvenient truth is the foundation of a thriving commercial ecosystem on Facebook and TikTok: Fake doctors, unregistered supplements, and "miracle" pills sold to people who are frightened, tired, or simply priced out of regular care.
Social media is filled with products claiming to replace insulin or conventional medication with herbal alternatives, despite no credible scientific evidence supporting those claims. Patients each month require hospitalization after following unqualified health advice found on social media and resulting in liver, kidney, or cardiovascular complications.
Think about what that number means. Families continue to pay for someone else's marketing copy with their organs. Now think about the patients who never made it to a hospital.
The word "herbal" does a great deal of the sellers' work. In a country with a long and respected tradition of traditional remedies, "natural" feels "safe." It is not.
A product with no declared dose, no tested purity, and no registration is simply an unknown substance. The danger is greatest when a patient stops a prescribed drug because a post told them they no longer need it.
What makes this scam distinctly Bangladeshi is how skilfully it borrows trust. Fraudsters know we respect the doctor, the professor, and the familiar newspaper masthead, so they counterfeit all three.
Dr Jahangir Kabir, a prominent health advocate who promotes lifestyle-based approaches to diabetes, has said dishonest groups are misusing his name to sell unregulated medicines.
He reports that hundreds of fake Facebook pages were created in his name, some even mimicking his verified profile's blue-badge image. A man who tells people to change how they eat and live found his face on the label of a bottle.
He is not alone. Microbiologist Dr Senjuti Saha discovered that her name and image were being used in a fraudulent campaign and filed a general diary at the police station.
Dismislab traced the "Optimax" diabetes product to counterfeit pages mimicking Prothom Alo, featuring fake interviews with "prominent" Bangladeshi professionals.
Even the health minister's identity has been hijacked: iIn 2024 the ministry had to warn that fake Facebook accounts were being opened in his name, with advertisements that could cheat the public.
When the scammer can wear the face of a trusted doctor and the logo of a trusted newspaper, "just don't believe everything online" is not advice. It is an abdication.
We have long assumed that more smartphones meant more awareness. The evidence is more troubling. Studies suggest that mobile phone ownership is associated with greater exposure to misinformation, not just greater access to information.
In a country where phones have reached the village before the specialist has, the same device that delivers a telemedicine consultation also delivers a "cure" for diabetes. In many cases, it is the second that arrives first.
Self-medication was already common long before Facebook. We buy tablets over the counter, trust a neighbour's prescription, and stretch a doctor's visit as far as it will go. Influencers did not create this habit. They have simply learned to monetize it.
Media professionals are not blameless. For years our response to health misinformation has been the occasional "myth-buster" column, published once, read by few, and forgotten by the next news cycle. The scammers publish daily. We cannot answer a daily campaign with an annual correction.
Newspapers need standing health fact-check desks, with trained reporters, a medical advisory panel, and the same institutional seriousness we give to political fact-checking. A fake diabetes ad should be treated with the same urgency as a fake political quote.
Television channels and online portals should produce short, shareable "spot the scam" segments in Bangla. Sixty seconds are enough to show a viewer how to check whether a doctor is registered with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council, why "cure in seven days" is a warning rather than a promise, and why no pill replaces insulin. Content that is easy to forward to the family WhatsApp group is how we compete on the scammers' own ground.
We should use AI sensibly. Newsrooms can deploy language tools, including Bangla-capable ones, to flag viral health claims, repeated ad creatives, and suspicious pages at a scale no human desk can match.
But AI should only flag. Verification, context, and the final call must remain with trained editors and doctors. A machine can tell us where the fire is. It cannot tell us whether the person in the video is really a physician.
Finally, the media must stop accepting the framing that this is merely a "content moderation" problem. Content moderation means a platform deciding whether a post stays up.
What we are describing is the sale of unregistered medicinal products, under false identities, to sick people, for profit. That is consumer fraud and a public health offense.
The Directorate General of Drug Administration, the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission, the consumer rights authorities and law enforcement all have a role.
So do Meta and TikTok, which earn revenue from the very advertisements that deceive our citizens.
The press should keep asking the uncomfortable questions: Who approved this ad, who was paid, who was prosecuted, and how many times was it reported before it came down?
The next time a "miracle cure" appears in your feed, remember what it is: Someone's sales pitch, aimed at your parent's fear.
Insulin is not a conspiracy, and diabetes does not end in seven days. The sooner we say so, loudly, every single day, the fewer families will learn it in a hospital corridor.
Dewan Shahnoor Alam Sourav is a lecturer in the Department of Media Studies and Journalism at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). Can be reached at ds.alam.sourav@gmail.com .

This is what I kept asking myself as I waited in the hospital, knowing that my 4.5-month pregnancy was coming to an end. Perhaps it is simply human nature to grow attached to the life growing inside you.
My entire life, I have catastrophized everything. The same happened when I found out I was pregnant. But I quickly tried to quiet that part of me and focus on doing my best.
Everything was going perfectly. I had no known risk factors, my scans had gone well, and my doctor had told me to schedule an appointment for the following month.
No one had warned me that even when everything seemed to be going well, it could all turn upside down in the blink of an eye.
I had gone to sleep when my amniotic fluid ruptured. Even half asleep, I knew what that meant. My pregnancy had ended. I was rushed to the hospital, and the duty doctor tried to console me: “We do not know yet.”
But I knew that the future I had already started imagining would no longer come to be.
I had to wait an excruciating 12 hours for my gynaecologist to examine me. She finally explained what would happen next. I would be given one dose of medication that day and more the following day to induce labour.
Miscarriage . Just one word, carrying a weight that is almost impossible to put into words. A grief so profound, yet one no one warns you about.
While I waited in the hospital for the procedures to be completed, my aunts, uncles, grandmothers, cousins, everyone, rallied around me. I was going through one of the most difficult periods of my life, but I was wrapped in a blanket of love.
The women around me told me their own stories of loss, their struggles, and how they had found a way through. Even though my own pain felt insurmountable, it was the strength I found in their stories that helped me through.
Despite medical science coming such a long way, no reason could be identified for why this was happening to me. The pregnancy was not advanced enough for there to be any hope of saving it, but it was also not early enough for my miscarriage to go unnoticed.
The medication I was given sent my body into what felt like a state of shock. I was shivering uncontrollably, and when the shivering stopped, my body would have to endure contractions. I had to feel the pain of labour, but there was no baby to hold at the end of it.
Nothing could be done to ease my pain, knowing that there was no possibility of a different ending. I was handed a death certificate for someone who never even had a birth certificate.
It is estimated that one in four to six pregnancies ends in miscarriage. But the statistics are complex. There are a multitude of factors that can play a role.
Most of the websites I have visited state that miscarriages are common. And this makes me question: Why is there so little conversation about something that affects women so deeply?
A pregnancy loss is deeply personal, and it should always be a woman’s prerogative to decide whether she wants to talk about it. But for those who do want to talk about it, do we have enough safe spaces?
There is so little mental health support for women going through a loss like this. I was genuinely grateful for the hospital staff who consoled me, who held my hand when my body was going through unbearable pain, and for the doctors who treated me with respect and dignity. But is that guaranteed for every woman who experiences a loss like this?
Too often, these losses are minimised with statements such as, “It was not meant to be.” As though a few words can make the grief disappear. We should hold space for women who are going through these losses and create more meaningful systems of support.
When even “rich” countries struggle to fund research into miscarriage and pregnancy loss, there is little hope for a country like Bangladesh.
The world can be an extremely cruel place for women. But I refuse to be anything but kind to myself.
There was a version of me that existed before the miscarriage, and there is a version of me that exists now. I do not think they are the same person.
The trivial things in life that used to bother me no longer seem to matter. Things I once thought were important have suddenly lost weight. There is something about losing something so deeply wanted that changes your understanding of what truly matters.
While I do not want my pregnancy loss to define me, I also cannot pretend that it is not a part of who I am now. I will carry this loss with me, and I will not allow it to be swept under the carpet or reduced to something that simply happened and should be forgotten.
I am still grieving the future I do not get to have. There is no linear path through a loss this profound. I was applauded for being brave, but the truth is, I was forced to be brave.
I no longer want to be courageous. I want to mourn. I want to grieve the life I never got to meet, on my own terms.
It is the strength of my parents, partner, and siblings that has kept me going. Life keeps moving forward, even though it felt like mine had stopped for a while.
The only lesson I carry forward is that I will show up with love, strength, and support for any woman who has gone through something similar. There should be more conversations about this reality, about a kind of loss that can be so profound and yet have no logical answers. Women should be allowed to grieve without being told how they should grieve.
Ahona Hassan is a human rights activist passionate about speaking on issues often left unspoken.

item.title: A collective failure. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The tragic loss of at least 20 young lives to suicide following the publication of this year’s SSC and HSC examination results -- including nine deaths within just ten days of the recent HSC announcement -- is a devastating indictment of our society.
Worse still, given the pervasive stigma surrounding mental health and self-harm across the country, these reported figures likely represent only a fraction of the true toll.
When teenagers choose to end their lives over academic scores, it exposes a profound moral and institutional collapse. That we live in a society where exam grades are treated as the sole determinant of human worth is a horrifying reality.
For decades, parents, educators, and communities have conditioned students to believe that falling short of a coveted GPA-5 or failing a board examination equates to absolute ruin. The relentless cycle of parental comparisons, social humiliation, and rigid academic expectations leaves vulnerable young minds isolated and terrified of disappointing their families.
When an examination hall becomes a matter of life and death, the entire pedagogical and social framework has fundamentally broken down. No board certificate is worth a single child's life, yet our culture continues to weaponize academic performance against the emotional well-being of our children.
This crisis demands immediate, structural intervention from both the state and society. We need accessible, confidential psychological counseling services in our educational institutions -- not as a formality, but as an active support network operating before and after exam seasons. Simultaneously, we must also expand emergency crisis helplines and train teachers to recognize early signs of acute distress and isolation.
Beyond policy, families must replace interrogation and shame with empathy and understanding, reassuring their children that academic setbacks are temporary obstacles, not life sentences.
If we continue to prioritize grades over emotional survival, these preventable tragedies will remain an annual stain on our national conscience. We must act now to protect our youth before another promising life is lost to despair.

Time to deliver to climate promises. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and UN General Assembly President Dr Khalilur Rahman both delivered what is an overdue message to the global community: The era of empty climate promises must end.
The prime minister rightly pointed out that climate-vulnerable nations require grants, not debt-inducing loans, all the while outlining five concrete actions to overhaul what must be called a broken international finance architecture.
Simultaneously, Dr Khalilur Rahman warned that the widening disparity between political pledges and real-world implementation has become an existential chasm, urging world leaders to make Antalya the "COP of implementation."
Nowhere is the hypocrisy displayed by the developed world more damaging than across developing countries of the Global South, and on the frontlines of our own country.
While global carbon emissions surged to a record 42 billion tons last year and warming trajectories hurtle toward 2.8 degrees Celsius for this century, developing economies continue bearing the catastrophic brunt of a crisis they did not create.
Bangladesh itself contributes less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet our coastal communities, river systems, and agricultural yields are being systematically dismantled by rising seas, salinity intrusion, and relentless cyclones.
The financial arithmetic outlined in Antalya lays bare the moral failure of major industrial polluters. Developing countries require up to $305 billion annually merely to adapt to climate fallout, yet international adaptation funding languishes at a paltry $26bn. As the UNGA president aptly noted, that shortfall is not a rounding error but a verdict on global solidarity.
If COP31 is to mean anything, wealthy nations must immediately honour their historical obligations. More international climate finance must be dedicated directly to adaptation, distributed as predictable grants based on vulnerability rather than arbitrary income classifications.
Antalya must not become another venue for hollow declarations. Major carbon-emitting powers must abandon stalling tactics and deliver the finance and action required to safeguard nations such as Bangladesh in the developing world.
